record.tranche_reason: The study measures downstream code-generation performance across training-token checkpoints, a different measure from scaling-law loss fits, and reports how performance changes with scale.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. for predictable language-modeling-loss relationships in related work, but does not test those laws. Its checkpoint performance results in Section 6.3 bear on V6. The 2K-versus-8K context perplexity comparison and cross-model benchmark comparisons do not test the claim versions.
record.test_reason: In a new setting (code LLMs), Section 6.3 reports downstream pass@1 for one 15.5B model at successive training-token checkpoints, and pass@1 against per-language data size. This bears on whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale (V6). The paper has no loss fits and no model-size sweep. T3 fits better than T2 because the study is a model report, not a method aimed at the scaling question.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors say longer training likely helps high-resource languages, while some low-resource languages improve little or decline (e.g. R between 800B and 1000B). They attribute this to available data size, since gains occur only for languages with ≳1 GB. They also note that R per-problem success varies erratically across checkpoints, with failures due to minor mistakes.
record.recipe_differences: A code-generation pass@1 checkpoint sweep for one 15.5B model, rather than held-out language-modeling-loss scaling-law fits or compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies by programming language and available data size; the paper notes that some low-resource languages improve little or decline.
record.problems: The checkpoint trend is reported mainly in a figure, with no uncertainty estimates stated for the claim-relevant results. The sweep concerns one model and pass@1 rather than held-out pretraining loss.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows retained. Cross-model benchmark comparisons do not isolate scaling, and the context-window perplexity comparison varies context length rather than model scale.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No small-run fits extrapolated to larger runs.
No shape ablation at fixed parameter count.
No power-law fits in other modalities or regimes; the code-domain results are downstream pass@1, not loss scaling.
No variation in model size. No relation of downstream performance to pretraining loss. No quantitative predictive fit across training tokens. No uncertainty estimates.
No comparison of fitted exponents or fitting choices.

missing.what: Pass@1 versus log per-language data size at each checkpoint. Linear fit R² ranges from 0.399 (600B) to 0.510 (1000B). Between 800B and 1000B the slope rises and the intercept falls, so gains are confined to languages with ≳1 GB of data.
Per-problem pass counts (out of 200) for R problems at the 400B/600B/800B/1000B checkpoints, showing large, apparently uncorrelated swings.

record.verdict_notes: The study is primarily a model-release report, and its link to the claim is weak. The 'scale' axis is training tokens within a single cosine-decay run, so intermediate checkpoints are not equivalent to separately trained token-optimal runs. The cross-model comparisons, e.g. StarCoder beating larger LLaMA and PaLM in Table 12, mix data and architecture and include cited numbers, so they are rightly excluded as rows. The 2K-versus-8K perplexity comparison varies context length, not scale. The paper cites Kaplan and Hoffmann only in related work.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or predictions for substantially larger runs.
No compute-budget allocation sweep or loss-minimising parameter/token split.
No controlled comparison of architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
No test of scaling-law form across other modalities or training regimes.
Tests code-generation pass@1 across training-token checkpoints, but not a relationship to pretraining loss or broad downstream-task predictability.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents, nor test of departures from fitted power laws.

rows.subject: StarCoderBase
rows.operation_detail: Measured pass@1 at checkpoints after successive amounts of training tokens.

conditions.value: several high-resource programming languages supported by MultiPL-E

rows.value: The curves for several high-resource languages suggest that longer training is likely to improve performance further.
rows.note: The authors describe the trend cautiously; individual plotted values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: Improvement with training tokens is visible in Figure 2 for high-resource languages, so the direction is observed. Predictability is not quantified: no fit over tokens and no values in the text. The checkpoints are intermediate points of one cosine-decay run, not separately trained runs, which confounds token scale with the learning-rate schedule.

rows.subject: StarCoderBase
rows.operation_detail: Measured pass@1 at checkpoints after successive amounts of training tokens.

conditions.value: some low-resource programming languages supported by MultiPL-E

rows.value: Some low-resource languages show limited improvement during training or a decline.
rows.note: The text reports a group-level pattern, without giving numerical values for each language.
rows.check: Group-level statement (limited improvement or decline). The specific languages and values are only in the figure, so this mixes partial and absent or reversed cases.

rows.subject: StarCoderBase
rows.operation_detail: Compared pass@1 across the 800B and 1000B training-token checkpoints.
rows.value: The pass@1 rate drops significantly between the 800B and 1000B checkpoints.
rows.note: The text explicitly describes a significant decline; numerical rates are not stated there.
rows.check: The value is correct per the text. numbers_found '2/2' is unexplained. Table D.3 gives per-problem pass counts that could quantify the drop.

relationships.condition: StarCoderBase, high-resource languages on MultiPL-E, 200B–1000B token checkpoints
relationships.reason: pass@1 rises with training tokens and the authors expect further gains (r1). The rise is shown in a figure only, with no predictive fit.
relationships.display_finding: pass@1 increased with training tokens, without a predictive fit.

relationships.condition: StarCoderBase, some low-resource languages (Figure 2 shows ≲1 GB data)
relationships.reason: These languages show limited improvement or declines with more tokens. The authors tie gains to having enough language data (r2).
relationships.display_finding: Additional training tokens produced limited gains or declines, which the authors linked to insufficient language data.

relationships.reason: R pass@1 drops significantly with more training tokens (r3).
relationships.display_finding: R pass@1 declined significantly between the 800B-token and 1000B-token checkpoints.

relationships.condition: Per-problem pass rates in R across 400B–1000B checkpoints
relationships.reason: Based on the text (Table D.3, no row): per-problem pass counts swing between checkpoints in an apparently uncorrelated way. Example: has_close_elements goes 197 to 5 of 200 between 800B and 1000B.
relationships.display_finding: Per-problem results fluctuated apparently independently across checkpoints; has_close_elements fell from 197 to 5 successful attempts out of 200 between 800B and 1000B tokens.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The checkpoint curves suggest performance improves with more training tokens in these languages (r1), though the text does not establish quantitative predictability.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The study reports limited improvement or declines for some languages rather than a uniform improvement with training tokens (r2).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: R pass@1 significantly decreases with additional training tokens (r3).
